subject: Biology
title: The World's Oldest Trees
description: One-minute skill: The World's Oldest Trees.

hook.text: A bristlecone pine named Methuselah has been alive for over 4,850 years—older than the pyramids.

buildup.text: These trees grow in harsh mountain conditions where thin air and poor soil slow competition.

discovery.text: Their dense, resinous wood resists rot, insects, and fungi that kill younger trees.

twist.text: An even older tree was cut down in 1964 by a researcher who didn't realize its age until too late.

climax.text: Ancient trees are living climate archives. Their rings record droughts, fires, and volcanic eruptions.

punchline.text: These trees were seedlings when writing was invented.

quiz.question: How old is the bristlecone pine named Methuselah?

details.summary: The oldest known living tree is a bristlecone pine over 4,800 years old in California's White Mountains. Clonal organisms like Pando, a quaking aspen colony in Utah, may be over 80,000 years old. These ancient plants have survived millennia of climate variation and disturbance.
details.whyItMatters: Ancient trees are living records of thousands of years of environmental change. Their growth rings provide climate data, and their survival strategies inform conservation. Their loss to climate change would be irreversible.
takeaways: Bristlecone pines in California are the oldest known individual trees at over 4,800 years
Pando is an aspen clone covering 43 hectares that may be over 80,000 years old
Growth rings in ancient trees record centuries to millennia of climate data

faq.question: How do bristlecone pines survive for thousands of years?
faq.answer: They grow in harsh high-altitude environments with little competition. Dense resinous wood resists rot and insects. Slow growth produces extremely hard wood. They can survive with only a strip of living bark, and dead wood remains standing for centuries protecting the living portion.

faq.question: Is Pando a single organism or many trees?
faq.answer: Pando is genetically a single organism, one vast root system that sends up individual tree stems across 43 hectares. All 47,000 stems are genetically identical clones connected underground. Though individual stems live about 130 years, the root system may be tens of thousands of years old.
